description: Hi! I'm Ralph Sean, a 14-year-old student from Infant Jesus Convent ISC School, Murukkumpuzha, India. I'm passionate about space, science and technology. I created Space Mission Designer for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to make space mission planning more interactive and fun to explore. From developing the idea to designing and building the simulation, this project has been a great learning experience. I'm excited to keep learning, experimenting and exploring new possibilities!
summary:
Space Mission Designer — “Design. Plan. Explore.” is an independent educational web app I created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. My goal is to make space mission planning easier to understand through an interactive experience where users can design, launch and explore their own missions.

Users build missions step by step by choosing objectives, destinations, spacecraft, instruments, propulsion, power and communication systems. They receive feedback through a six-dimension Mission DNA profile, four resource budgets, a rule-based Mission Advisor and a design check.

Once ready, users launch an eight-phase simulation with live system gauges, mission events, challenging decisions, scientific observations and communication delays based on one-way light time. Each mission ends with one of five outcome levels and a report explaining what happened and why. A Failure Investigator helps users understand mission problems.

The What-If, Robustness and Replay labs allow users to test different designs and compare results. The app also features real mission profiles of Voyager 1 and Cassini–Huygens, a learning library and an optional learning check.

Built with Next.js, React and TypeScript, it uses public NASA reference sources. Only one-way light time and inverse-square solar intensity are physically calculated; other scores and simulation results are educational models, not real engineering predictions.
details:
Space Mission Designer — Design. Plan. Explore.

Space Mission Designer is an independent educational project I created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The idea came from a simple thought: instead of just reading about how space missions work, why not let people design one and experience the challenges themselves?

In a real space mission, every decision matters. Choosing a spacecraft, power source or communication system can affect the entire mission. I wanted to make these connections easier to understand through an interactive experience.

Users begin by building a mission across nine guided stages. They choose a scientific objective, destination, spacecraft, instruments, propulsion, power and communication systems. As they make decisions, the app provides feedback through Mission DNA, which measures six aspects of the design, four resource budgets for mass, power, propellant and data, and a rule-based Mission Advisor. It also checks the design, distinguishing between missing requirements and choices that may cause problems during the mission.

Once the mission is ready, users can launch an eight-phase simulation. It features six live system gauges, mission events, unexpected challenges and decisions involving trade-offs. Scientific observations depend on the instruments selected, while communication delays are based on calculated one-way light time. This means the choices made during mission design can directly affect what happens during flight.

At the end, users receive one of five mission outcomes, along with a report explaining what went well, what went wrong and what could be improved. The Failure Investigator and Causal Investigation help users explore the reasons behind the results using evidence from their mission.

There is more to explore after the simulation. The What-If Lab lets users change one design choice and compare results. The Robustness Lab tests designs across multiple runs using matched random seeds, while Replay allows users to explore how changing a decision affects a mission. The project also includes sourced profiles of Voyager 1 and Cassini–Huygens, a seven-topic learning library and an optional learning check.

The application is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript. It uses publicly available NASA, NASA JPL and other space-science reference sources. To keep the science honest, it calculates only one-way light time and solar intensity using the inverse-square law. Other scores, budgets and simulation outcomes are simplified educational models, not real engineering predictions.

Space Mission Designer is not an official NASA or ESA product, nor is it an engineering-grade mission simulator. My aim is to make space science more interactive and help learners discover how much thought, planning and teamwork goes into exploring space.
